COOLING / PRACTICAL ENERGY GUIDE

How much electricity does an air conditioner use?

An air conditioner drawing a steady 1,200 W uses 1.2 kWh per hour. At an example price of $0.16/kWh, four equivalent full-power hours per day cost $23.04 over 30 days.

Illustrative figures · USD · Replace the example rate with your own

Find the electrical input

Look for electrical input power in watts (W) or kilowatts (kW) on the label, manual, or specification sheet. For this calculation, 1.2 kW of electrical input means 1,200 W.

Cooling capacity is a different measurement. A figure in BTU per hour, or a kW figure labeled cooling capacity, describes cooling output. It cannot be entered directly as the electricity consumed. ENERGY STAR lists room air-conditioner cooling capacity in BTU per hour and recommends selecting an appropriate capacity for the room.

If the specification lists an input range, actual draw can change with operating conditions. A single rated input is a simplified scenario; measured energy gives a more specific estimate for your unit.

Work out the energy cost

1,200 ÷ 1,000 × 4 × $0.16 × 30 = $23.04

This example uses 4.8 kWh daily and 144 kWh over 30 days. The hourly cost while drawing 1,200 W is $0.192, which rounds to $0.19 for display. Use the unrounded value when calculating a longer period.

Replace the watts, operating time, and rate with your own figures. If electricity is priced differently by time of day, calculate each rate period separately and add the costs.

Handle cycling and variable power

A conventional compressor may alternate between running and stopping as the room reaches its target temperature. A variable-speed unit may adjust its electrical draw instead. Time switched on and time at rated input can therefore differ.

For an illustrative eight-hour session, assume a 1,200 W compressor draws that power for half the time. Four equivalent full-power hours give a compressor-only estimate of 4.8 kWh. A fan or other components may add consumption.

An alternative is to use average input measured over the full session. An average of 600 W across eight hours also gives 4.8 kWh. Use either average power with total time, or running power with equivalent hours, without reducing both for the same cycling effect.

Compare example usage

Illustrative steady electrical inputs at $0.16/kWh; not ratings of particular models
Electrical inputEquivalent hours/dayDaily energy30-day cost
800 W4 hours3.2 kWh$15.36
1,200 W4 hours4.8 kWh$23.04
1,200 W8 hours9.6 kWh$46.08
2,000 W4 hours8 kWh$38.40

The 1,200 W example costs twice as much at eight equivalent full-power hours as at four. Actual usage depends on the unit and conditions, so these examples help compare assumptions rather than forecast every hot day.

Use measured energy when available

If a suitable energy monitor or your equipment reports 5 kWh for a day's cooling, multiply that directly by your rate: 5 × $0.16 = $0.80. Thirty days at that same consumption would cost $24.00.

Check whether the measurement covers only the air conditioner or a larger circuit. Central-system fan energy may need to be included separately. Compare several representative days rather than treating one day's reading as a fixed yearly pattern.
